I lean Kafka, but it depends on what the notifications actually need. If we need ordering per recipient, replay, and a durable log a few consumers read at their own pace, Kafka. That's where my production experience is: I moved booking events from RabbitMQ to Kafka at Tessarine, and on Skeinrouter I used 48 partitions keyed by shipment ID to keep per-entity ordering, with idempotent consumers. If instead it's moderate fan-out where per-message retry and routing matter more than replay, RabbitMQ is less machinery to run. I'd size it on how much ordering and replay we actually need.

[[GIST]] Kafka when ordering and replay matter

Mine was the partition key for Skeinrouter, our tracking pipeline. Ilakkiya, a staff engineer on Platform, reviewed the design and wanted the main topic keyed by carrier ID so per-carrier rate limiting fell out for free. I wanted **shipment ID**, because our top three carriers produce about 38% of events, so carrier keys meant a few very hot partitions. We argued in doc comments for a week and got nowhere. What settled it was data. I replayed two days of production traffic through both schemes, and with carrier keys the busiest partition ran 14 minutes behind at peak, against 2 seconds with shipment keys. Her rate-limiting point was still right, so I built a per-carrier throttle into the webhook delivery layer.

[[GIST]] partition key dispute settled with data

The cleanest answer is that a table should have one owning service, and the other one goes through it. So I'd pick the service that owns the data model and the invariants, and have the second service call its API or consume its events instead of writing directly. If both genuinely need to write, I'd split the table so each owns its own columns or rows, or put a single writer in front of both. The thing I'd avoid is two services writing the same rows, because then nobody owns the constraints and you get races and inconsistent state.

[[GIST]] one owner, others go through it
